Well, thank you very much, and I'm very honoured to share the stage here with my good friends Emmanuel and Pedro. And thank you to Emmanuel for acknowledging Australia's leading role in this. There are too many parents who have lost their sons and daughters in the most extreme examples of the impact of social media. and the power of drama that was the Adolescents program produced in the UK highlighted the fact that people did not know what was going on when a bedroom door was shut. The truth is that it's been very well received by parents because it's enabled, whilst some children, as we said when we introduced the legislation, young people are smart. Some of them will work out ways to get around technology, but we couldn't allow the perfect to be the enemy of the good. And we know that the impact of social media has led to an increase in mental health issues. It's leading to an addiction to algorithms and scrolling. It's leading to further anxieties, eating disorders and behavioural issues, which is essentially robbing children of their childhood. And we want to give it back to them. We want children to learn how to interact with each other face to face, rather than to think their best friend is a bot or a non-existent production of AI online. It is the opposite of that. It is about giving everyone control over their own lives. and it's an inevitable next stage, because whilst today we're concentrating on the impact on children, the truth is this is having an impact on our entire society and how it functions, with misinformation, disinformation, with the increased polarisation that we're seeing as well in the political system, where people are moving away from the centre and more and more to the extremes, be they of the left or the right. All of these controls can be done. When we first proposed a social media ban, they said, oh, we can't tell how old people are. The truth is that some of these companies, like Meta, have more information about young people than their parents do. That is the truth of the matter. They have been able to comply, and they should comply. In July, I also announced the third part of our legislation, which we will do by the end of this year, which is Australian standards for AI. So we need to shape the technology rather than allow the technology to shape us. For all of our faults is part of what makes us human, the idea. As some have argued, that AI will create perfection. is something that is, I think, very misdirected. Because if we leave it like, I think, We did on social media, as Pedro and Emmanuel have both said as well. We should have moved earlier. Let's not make the same mistake. Let's learn from it and make sure that we shape AI in the interests of humanity. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Your Excellency Macron, President of France. I want to thank all the other colleagues that have spoken before me. On a safer digital space for minors. Its message is important. Protecting children requires responsibility. Not only from families and governments, but also from those who design and operate the technologies children use. Children do not experience technology in the same way everywhere. Connectivity, devices, language, digital literacy, parental support, and the capacity of institutions to protect them vary greatly across countries and communities. This matters especially for developing countries. For millions of children, technology is a pathway to education, knowledge, healthcare, and opportunity. The digital divide remains real. Our answer, therefore, cannot be to deny children access. We must expand access and make technology safer by design. Countries are developing different approaches to age assurance, platform responsibility, and the protection of minors. Through the Children Act, our child protection policies, and our national AI strategy 2025 to 2030, we are strengthening the foundation for a safer digital environment. First of all, striking figures from the Eurobarometer that we had in July, 92% of Europeans say engage more in protecting children online, 92%. So people have understood what's going on. Another figure I want to share with you, Pedro mentioned it, on average European minors spend four to six hours a day on screen. But there's a second feature that is important. It was built with capture attention in mind and monetize this attention. If you look at the Meta settlement, It speaks volumes for itself that Meta is admitting not having… having protected children enough. They created the algorithm. For me, the most important part in this law was and is that we reverse the burden of proof. Very tedious process, very difficult, takes month and month and month. Then we argue with the platform. They say they will change a little bit. Again, months and months are passing by. And in the end, after three, four, five years, you have perhaps a fine that is being paid. but you didn't really have an influence on a generation that has grown and passed since then. Thank you. Next, we have His Excellency, Mr. Alar Karis, President of Estonia. Your Excellency, how is Estonia approaching this? And what are the key measures you are considering? And what do you expect from the coalition on this important topic?

Thank you very much, and Excellencies, delegates, and dear friends. Allow me to start with saying that Estonia, innovation and protection must go together. And Estonia does not see protecting children and enabling innovation as competing objectives. Both have to advance together. AI will be part of children education, future workplaces and everyday lives. Our responsibility is therefore not simply to shield children from technology, but to equip them to use it safely, critically, and confidently. Children's rights, safety, and well-being should be considered from the very beginning of AI design and deployment, rather than addressed only after harm occurs. And technology alone cannot solve technology-related harms. Teachers, parents, and other trusted adults remain essential. And children and young people themselves should have a meaningful role in shaping the technologies, policies, and safeguards that affect them. And some concrete measures. AI Leap. Estonia's AI Leap is a concrete example of this approach. We have chosen to shape and lead the use of AI in education. rather than simply react to it. AI Leap is not about access to technology. It is equally about AI literacy, teachers' capacity, pedagogy, and responsible implementation. And we started with upper secondary school students for different reasons, and now we continue with primary school. And the aim of the students is to become conscious, critical and self-directed users of AI, using it to support thinking and learning rather than to replace what I said already. Implementation should be evidence-based. We need to understand how AI affects learning outcomes, critical thinking, social development and children well-being. Privacy. Data protection and cybersecurity must be built into the systems children use from the outset. At the same time, we need to address emerging AI-related risks, including deepfakes, sexualized synthetic content, and algorithmically amplified harmful material. Now, a final question was what Estonia expects from a coalition. We would like the coalition to help move the international discussion from principles to practical implementation. It can provide a platform for governments to share evidence, lessons learned, and good practices on how to protect children's rights while enabling them to benefit from AI. And the coalition should help develop practical guidance for policymakers and those designing and deploying AI systems used by children. It should also bring together government, international organizations, technology companies, researchers, civil societies, educators, parents, and importantly, children and young people themselves. And no country can address these challenges alone. A coalition can help turn successful national approaches into solutions and safeguards that can be applied more widely. Thank you very much.

We have Dr. Matilde Cereoli, the co-founder and chief scientist of Everyone AI, and also one of the lead architects for IREES, the International Coalition for Beneficial AI for Children. Thank you. Excellencies, delegates, and colleagues, today's generation is the first that will never know a world without AI. And their brains are still developing, shaping how they will think, relate, and understand themselves. How these technologies interact with them will influence who they grow up to be. So that is the first thing I want to leave you with. We cannot let AI hinder children's cognitive and social emotional development. The decision we are making will shape whether 20 years from now we look back and see AI as a tool that helped a generation grow or wish we had made different choices when we still had the time. The effect of AI on children's development may be gradual. And the evidence will take years to build, but we do not have the luxury of waiting because millions of children are already interacting with this technology and some risk we anticipated two years ago are no longer hypothetical. Following President Macron's G7 call for scientific contribution, we mapped how generative AI could affect child development. More than 60 researchers have endorsed it. It showed two things. Early scientific consensus is possible, and it should guide design, because design is where the difference lies between a product that supports a child development and one that starts building emotional and cognitive overreliance. Without purposeful, evidence-based design, we risk making two mistakes at the same time, creating harms we could have prevented and missing the opportunities we could have built. That's why at EveryoneAI, we are measuring how those anthropomorphic systems behave toward a child to drive research and product safety implementation. But no one actor can do this alone. Through IRIS, co-led with the Paris Peace Forum, we have built an international network that can support this coalition effort, bringing together governments, frontier AI companies, more than 100 researchers, 15 GOs like EdSafe Alliance and Common Sense Media, and youth voices. What we need now is government action to turn these measures into standards companies have to meet and invest in the research needed to keep improving them. Because what happens in the digital world does not stay there. It shapes children, the adult they become, and the societies they build. Thank you.

Thank you so much for having me. Greatly appreciate the remarks, President Macron, Prime Minister Sanchez, Prime Minister Albanese, Prime Minister Callus, President Ruto, President von der Leyen. This is consistent with the technology that is designed to help people to learn, to think, to create, to produce, and to build. Very much look forward to seeing the Kids Act and how that gets translated into concrete actions. In the EU, strongly support the work of the Commission. One of the things that we've suggested as we've gone along here is, you know, there are these AI safety institutes that we work with from around the world. There's one here in the U.S., the U.K., many of the countries represented here. A thought that I would like to proffer for this distinguished group is, could we think about an AI safety institute specific specifically for children, that would help serve as an organizing tool for the world. And then I think we have to think about the opportunity that is here. If you think about those general purpose technologies, perhaps the one that this is very akin to is the printing press. and thinking of the direction that the world went in between those countries that leaned in and became very literate and those countries that maybe did not. How do you see the orchestration between different stakeholders, between states, companies, and civil society, and the UN on child protection in the age of AI? Monsieur le President Macron.

Mr. President, the security and the well-being of children should very much be rooted in the development of these technologies. Protecting children is already to some extent organized, but there's a risk about their threats for the dignity of children or that their trust might be abused. We need to take into account the development of the child and preserve their right to private life. The governments have a responsibility in organizing an efficient protection, and technology companies should also be responsible for the consequences of their decisions on children and take into account their safety when they design products or services. Artificial intelligence is opening new opportunities, make education more accessible, and make and overcome a number of obstacles and make sure that everyone can fully contribute to society. This opportunity should also contribute to helping the children who have special needs. And we should also work on reducing inequalities in getting access to knowledge and technology development. Families and teachers have a major role to play, and they should, to that extent, be supported and be put in a position to help their children develop their own opinions and act responsibly. The opinions of the children themselves should also be heard and taken on board, based on their age and their maturity. Their experience is essential for the decisions impacting their daily lives and their future. Excellencies, Bulgaria commend the opportunity given to us to make the best of UNESCO's capacity and expertise in that field. These are international challenges which require continuous cooperation, and the coalition can indeed bring some practical contributions when it comes to sharing knowledge and put in place appropriate approaches, including for countries with less opportunities. And for Bulgaria, the purpose of this cooperation is that each child should be allowed to grow up in a safe environment and make the best of technological progress in order to develop their capacities and build the best possible life. Thank you for your attention.

Your Excellency, I'd now like to bring in Mr. Jim Steer, the CEO of Common Sense Media. Jim, we have heard from co-chairs that protecting children in the age of AI is a critical topic of governments. What do you think states should be doing to protect children in the age of AI?

First of all, thank you so much for having us here today. Monsieur Macron, merci beaucoup for your leadership. C'est fantastique.

Thank you for your fantastic leadership, President Macron.

McCall, you have Prime Minister Sanchez, you have Prime Minister Albanese, you have President von der Leyen talking about the importance of children in the AI age. This is the first time this has happened on a world stage at this scale, in this way. That is a remarkable moment, and that is remarkable leadership. Look, children -- and some of you will have grandchildren soon, too. Your children and grandchildren are going to be the people who experience the world of AI. They are going to be the beneficiaries or the people who suffer the consequences of how we develop this extraordinary technology. And today is a huge milestone because what it represents is a global movement of people at the highest level of society, but also across all levels of society, that kids and families need to come first in the age of AI. And it is very important that the world leaders are recognizing that. So as Mr. Lehane, my friend over there, mentioned, The U.S. actually has great leadership in this area. It's just not from Washington. It's from California, which is where the country -- where the companies are all based. And we just passed, over the objections of many of the big tech companies, major, important legislation that protects children in the way that President von der Leyen's Kids Act and some of the work that President Macron and others have done in Europe, and also mirroring what President -- Prime Minister Albanese has done. So I think this is a game changing moment for the public and for children in particular. So we look at this, if you look at the issues of children versus the big tech giants, most of which are American companies, we know that. This is the story of David versus Goliath. But I would just like to remind you who won. David won. And that is what is going to happen here too. So I will tell you again, David beat Goliath. Children and grandchildren are going to win here, and common sense will prevail. Thank you very much. Merci beaucoup.

Thank you, Jim. And I'd now like to bring in Ms. Erin Mote, the CEO of InnovateEDU. Erin, as we navigate this critical juncture in AI development, how do we move past the false choice between innovation and safety to build a globally accountable ecosystem for our children?

Jim's right. We gather at a defining crossroads in managing AI's promise and peril. The conversation around artificial intelligence and our children is too often a false binary, innovation versus protection. But safety is not the counterpolarity to innovation. Safety is the foundation upon which true innovation stands. If we build AI systems that compromise the next generation's well-being, we are not innovating. We are mortgaging our future. To move from aspiration to accountability, we must anchor our work in three critical imperatives. First, we need an independent ecosystem of third party evaluators and auditors. As President Mark Kroll rightly emphasized, tech companies cannot self-regulate. Developers cannot mark their own homework. The EdSafe AI Alliance is a global initiative powered by a coalition of stakeholders across the education sector. We're helping to set the agenda for ecosystems alongside multilateral organizations, research institutions, and governments. By championing safe by design principles anchored in our safe framework, safety, accountability, fairness, transparency, and efficacy, we ensure products are transparent and accountable before they ever reach a classroom or a child's hand. Second, as you have heard of the call from the I-RAISE coalition, of which EdSafe is a part, whose critical work in building cohesion and collaboration is essential to ensuring we have global coherence around a shared research agenda. Fragmented national approaches leave gaps where our most vulnerable fall through. AI literacy, evidence, and research must be the cornerstone of our ability to look a parent, an educator, a child in the eye and say, we will protect you. Third, we must champion global collaborations, such as this coalition and the work that EdSafe AI is doing with the University of Oxford. We're building vital connective tissue between researchers, educators, families, and governments. Global AI safety requires moving past borders and boardrooms. This collaboration cannot be limited to the countries where frontier models are developed. From Pakistan's remote villages to Barcelona's classrooms and Nairobi's vibrant neighborhoods, 120 diverse EdSafe AI fellows are leading this work where it matters most. No single actor, sector, or hemisphere can solve this alone. This is our clarion call for global action. The digital world is an environment where our children live, learn, and grow, including my two children, Robert and Claire. Let us commit today to building a digital ecosystem worthy of their potential, anchored in trust, safety, and transparency. Thank you.

Thank you, Erin. Finally, we have a joint intervention from the UN agencies. Her Excellency, Ms. Doreen Bogdan-Martin, Secretary General of the ITU. His Excellency, Mr. Khaled El-Anani, Director General of UNESCO. Her Excellency, Ms. Catherine Russell, Executive Director of UNICEF, and His Excellency, Mr. Volker, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.

Excellencies, let me thank our leaders from France, Spain, Kenya, and Australia for bringing us together today. Jim, I too believe this is a remarkable moment, and as you said, a game-changing moment. We are here because we believe that every child should be able to benefit from AI without having to bear risks that they cannot understand or control. ITU is proud to join the launch of this coalition, and today we offer the coalition three contributions, drawing on nearly two decades of ITU's work in child online protection. The first is technical expertise. We can advance technical standards for safety and privacy by design, including age assurance, and work with partners to address AI-generated abuse, deepfakes, and non-consensual intimate imagery. Second, support in countries. Working with UNICEF, UNESCO, OCHR and governments, we can bring guidance and practical tools together with particular attention to programs in developing countries. We can also help reinforce the skills that parents and educators need to recognize the risks and use artificial intelligence with confidence while ensuring, of course, that children themselves have a meaningful voice in shaping these programs. And third, coordination that leads to action. The UN Interagency Working Group on Artificial Intelligence that is co-led by ITU and UNESCO offers a way to connect expertise across the UN system, including the Committee on the Rights of the Child, and to mobilize and to track voluntary commitments to this coalition's roadmap. ITU can leverage its Partner to Connect platform to turn our shared roadmap into action. Ladies and gentlemen, we must, we must do everything that we can to make AI worthy of our children and their caregivers. We owe it to them through safer products, stronger protections, and meaningful participation. That is the power and the responsibility of this coalition. You can count on ITU support every step of the way.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I thank leaders of France, Kenya, Australia, and Spain for bringing us together around this very important, remarkable moment, as Jim said. UNESCO is ready to contribute to this coalition, first as a standard setter. In 2021, UNESCO's member states adopted the recommendation on the ethics of artificial intelligence, the first global normative framework on AI. Second, as a policy advisor, having worked with some 80 countries to translate its principles into policies and practices. Third, as a capacity builder, with expertise in training more than 25,000 teachers, students, content creators, civil servants, judges on ethical AI. Fourth, as a trusted platform for dialogue, UNESCO will continue bringing together government, companies, civil society, families, and young people. path by mobilizing UNESCO global networks of experts, university chairs, research institutes, and associated schools around the world. And we published last June with our partners in France a guide, practical guide for parents to enforce the dialogue with their children. Finally, we are exploring now with our member states a new normative instrument to empower and protect children and young people for the age of AI. For this reason, UNESCO supports the roadmap and propose working on the thematic working group on AI literacy, digital literacy and critical thinking. Together with our partners, UNICEF, ITU and OCHR, we can connect principles of expertise and concrete action to deliver tangible results for children and young people. Thank you.

Oh, great. Thank you so much, President Macron. Thank you. Nice to see you. Excellencies, thank you for inviting UNICEF to be here today. So this past July in Geneva, UNICEF helped launch the Coalition for Children's Rights and Protection in the Age of Artificial Intelligence. Today is an important step forward in the direction of protecting children. But we all know that the simple truth here is that children are not waiting for us to make up our minds about AI. They're already using it. On the one hand, opportunities of AI are enormous for children. It can help children learn, create, and access information and services that were once out of reach. UNICEF is fully engaged in those efforts, but the risks are real too. Our research found that in just one year across 11 countries, at least 1.2 million children had their images turned into sexually explicit deepfakes. And despite the name, there is nothing fake about the harm these things cause for children. AI must be designed with children's safety and rights in mind from the very beginning, which means that we are already behind. This coalition can help us do three things. First, put safety and child rights at the heart of AI design. Second, build better evidence about how AI affects children's learning, development, mental health, and well-being. And third, give children a voice in the decision shaping their digital lives while ensuring that every child can benefit from these technologies. UNICEF brings global experience, evidence, children's perspectives to this work. But while regulation is critical here, there is no government, no agency, or no company that can do this alone. We all bear the responsibility to keep children, their rights, and their needs at the center of the AI discussion. Thank you very much.

Government, thank you for organizing this important event.

...The last to be asked about it. So my office asked them. Together with our partners, we surveyed more than 1,000 children in 49 countries about their concerns around AI. And children told us they worry about AI being used to create fake images of real people, to exploit their private data, to reduce their creativity, and to replace real-life relationships with their families, friends, teachers, or therapists. Crucially, they want to be heard before decisions are taken, not after. Is this happening? Are children being heard? The Convention on the Rights of the Child is the most widely ratified human rights treaty in the world today. It is, one should also mention, legally binding, not just for states, but with clear responsibilities for the corporate sector and in particular the tech companies. The duty to respect children's rights and all our rights lies with those building AI. It includes human rights due diligence before release, transparency, and independent verification. And it relies on governments enforcing laws. Voluntary commitments are simply not enough. There is also fundamentally a question of responsibility and accountability. We welcome very much the coalition's roadmap. pointing to international guidance on rights-based AI for children and young people, every AI product needs to be required to clear a high bar before it reaches a child. We all are there to support these efforts and you have heard all our voices and there is one clear message. Children's rights apply to AI as they apply everywhere. Thank you.
